claims.text: Dynamic mechanical behavior in solidified Co-free FeNiCrMn is primarily governed by a temperature- and strain-rate-dependent transition between dislocation glide and deformation twinning.
Lower temperatures reduce dislocation mobility and thereby promote deformation twinning in FeNiCrMn.
Higher strain rates reduce effective dislocation mobility and thereby promote deformation twinning in FeNiCrMn.
Deformation twins impede dislocation motion and increase strength in FeNiCrMn.
Twinning provides auxiliary plastic strain and therefore preserves ductility while strengthening FeNiCrMn.
At higher temperatures, dislocation glide and dynamic recovery become the predominant deformation processes in FeNiCrMn.
At lower strain rates, dislocation glide and dynamic recovery become the predominant deformation processes in FeNiCrMn.
The as-solidified equiatomic or near-equiatomic FeNiCrMn microstructure is likely a single-phase solid solution.
The relative density and distribution of deformation twins and dislocation substructures mediate the mechanical response across temperature and strain-rate conditions.
Low-temperature or high-strain-rate deformation will produce a higher density of deformation twins.
Low-temperature or high-strain-rate deformation will produce increased flow stress.
Higher-temperature or lower-strain-rate deformation will produce less twinning and more continuous dislocation glide.
Higher-temperature or lower-strain-rate deformation will result in lower flow stress and greater ductility.
The glide-to-twinning transition will map systematically onto changes in measured stress-strain curves.
Room-temperature, moderate-strain-rate FeNiCrMn has a strength-ductility balance comparable to CoCrFeMnNi.
Extensive secondary-phase formation, recrystallization, brittle fracture, or defect engineering can move the alloy outside the regime governed by glide-twinning competition.
The relative contributions of twinning and dislocation glide may vary with processing history, composition, and grain size.
Dynamic strain aging or precipitation could modify the proposed deformation behavior.
Failure to observe systematic changes in twinning, dislocation structures, and mechanical response across temperature and strain rate would falsify the proposed controlling mechanism.
